title: Gujarat's Swaminarayan
hook: a teacher writes a short letter of daily conduct for people he'll never meet

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gujarat's Swaminarayan: the Vachanamrut, a scripture that began as questions in a courtyard. Did you ask someone a real question, and hear the whole answer? Day one thousand four hundred three.

A conversation only reaches the people in the courtyard. So what about everyone else? The farmer three villages over who couldn't come. The family that moved away for work. The devotee who'll be born long after the teacher is gone. Swaminarayan's answer, tradition says, was to write a letter. Not a long book of philosophy. A short one, in verse, that a person could carry, read, and actually live by. It's called the Shikshapatri. And the thing that makes it unusual isn't only what it says. It's how it asks to be used. Today, a letter written to people the writer would never meet.
screen: `THE ONES WHO COULDN'T COME.` → `A SHORT LETTER IN VERSE.` → `MEANT TO BE CARRIED.`

segments.voice: Shiksha means instruction, teaching. Patri is a letter. So the Shikshapatri is, quite plainly, a letter of instruction. Swaminarayan followers hold it as his own writing, and it reads like guidance from someone who knows what an ordinary day looks like. Begin with what it asks. In paraphrase, it asks followers not to harm living beings, not to eat meat or drink alcohol, not to steal, not to lie, and to be careful with harsh speech. It speaks about serving one's parents and giving to those in need. Much of it is everyday conduct: what you eat, how you speak, how you keep a household. Next, who it's for. It has guidance for householders and for sadhus, for married women and for widows, even for rulers. It doesn't pretend everyone lives the same life. Each gets guidance that fits. And last, the part worth noticing: how it asks to be used. The letter asks to be read every day. And for those who can't read, it asks that they listen to it read aloud, with respect. So the letter carries its own instructions for being kept alive. A teaching that stays only in a book on a shelf can fade. A teaching read every morning becomes part of the morning. That's the bet the Shikshapatri makes: that small, steady contact with good words shapes a life more than one big moment of inspiration.
screen: `SHIKSHAPATRI — A LETTER OF INSTRUCTION` · `EVERYDAY CONDUCT, PLAINLY SAID` · `GUIDANCE THAT FITS EACH LIFE` · `READ IT EVERY DAY`

segments.voice: One line, kept. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of one line of good counsel you've been given in your life, from a parent, a teacher, a book, a friend. Let it come back in the words you remember. Say it once, quietly, in your mind. Then just sit with it, the way someone might sit with the morning reading before the day starts. If it slips away, bring it back gently. If you pray, you can hold that line before God. The bell holds the time.
Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, the Shikshapatri, his short letter of everyday conduct, meant to be read, or heard, every day. Today's word.
Your line: Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, come back to that one line of good counsel three times: morning, midday, and before you sleep. Day one thousand four hundred three.

howItsDone: The Shikshapatri asks Swaminarayan devotees to read it daily, and it is read aloud and explained at gatherings for those who listen rather than read.

fork.setup: you're a teacher writing for followers you'll never meet, some of whom can't read. how do you keep your letter alive?
options: make it long, so nothing is left out.
ask that it be read daily, and read aloud for those who can't read.
keep it in one temple for safekeeping.
fork.reveal: the Shikshapatri asks to be read every day, and heard read aloud by those who can't read it themselves.
